implementation_notes: Suspending functions are language syntax, so structured concurrency is the idiomatic realization: inside a coroutineScope or supervisorScope, one async per recipient is the fan-out and awaitAll() is the wait-for-all gather, with withTimeoutOrNull(budget) supplying the deadline as a nullable result instead of an exception so the partial merge can continue. A plain coroutineScope cancels every sibling on the first failure, which is the failure-intolerant policy; supervisorScope plus per-async error handling is the partial-result policy. The scope - not the developer - owns the task lifetimes, so nothing leaks past the gather.
pitfalls: coroutineScope cancels all siblings when one async fails; use supervisorScope and handle each Deferred's exception (or runCatching inside the async) for a partial gather.
awaitAll rethrows the first failure and withTimeoutOrNull returns null with no per-recipient detail - a gather that must explain the partial answer needs results streamed through a Channel instead.
async without a dispatcher/limit is not back-pressure: bounding the fan-out width requires a Semaphore or a limited dispatcher.

variants.name: Flow merge() with first-acceptable selection
variants.implementation_notes: When the answers are streamed rather than one-shot, the aggregator becomes a flow operator: merge(flows) emits every answer as it arrives and first { it.acceptable } implements the first-success policy, with the budget applied by the enclosing withTimeout. Flow's structured cancellation tears the losing upstreams down as soon as the collector completes, which is closer to 'merge the answers that arrive in time' than awaitAll is. For a single request/response fan-out the async/awaitAll form is still the simpler realization; merge is the right tool for long-lived subscriptions or progressive answers.
pitfalls: merge interleaves without ordering or deduplication: the same answer can arrive from two recipients and both are emitted, so acceptability must be checkable per emission.
The losing upstreams are cancelled only when the collector terminates; a missing timeout leaves the merge open forever and holds every subscription.
